questions.corrige_markdown:
The terms $3\left(\dfrac14\right)^r$ for $r = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ form a geometric progression with first term and common ratio

$$a = 3\cdot\frac14 = \frac34, \qquad \rho = \frac14.$$

Since $|\rho| = \dfrac14 < 1$, the series converges and its sum to infinity is $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - \rho}$:

$$S_\infty = \frac{3/4}{1 - 1/4} = \frac{3/4}{3/4} = 1.$$

$$\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} 3\left(\frac14\right)^r = 1}$$

(Check: partial sums $0.75,\ 0.9375,\ 0.984375,\ \dots$ approach $1$. Alternatively, $3\sum_{r\ge1}(1/4)^r = 3\cdot\dfrac{1/4}{3/4} = 3\cdot\dfrac13 = 1$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a series is given by $S_n = 2n^2 + n$. Find an expression for the $n^{th}$ term of the series. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The $n^{th}$ term is the difference of consecutive partial sums: $u_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 2$, and $u_1 = S_1$.

$$S_{n-1} = 2(n-1)^2 + (n-1) = 2n^2 - 4n + 2 + n - 1 = 2n^2 - 3n + 1.$$

$$u_n = (2n^2 + n) - (2n^2 - 3n + 1) = 4n - 1, \qquad n \ge 2.$$

For $n = 1$: $u_1 = S_1 = 2 + 1 = 3$, and the formula $4n - 1$ also gives $3$, so it holds for all $n \ge 1$:

$$\boxed{u_n = 4n - 1}$$

(Check: $u_1 + u_2 + u_3 = 3 + 7 + 11 = 21 = 2(9) + 3 = S_3$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a series is given by $S_n = 2n^2 + n$. Show that the series is an arithmetic progression. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
From part (ii)(a), $u_n = 4n - 1$ for all $n \ge 1$. For every $n \ge 1$,

$$u_{n+1} - u_n = \bigl(4(n+1) - 1\bigr) - (4n - 1) = 4,$$

a constant independent of $n$. A sequence whose consecutive terms differ by a constant is an arithmetic progression, so the series is an arithmetic progression with first term $a = 3$ and common difference $d = 4$: $3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + \cdots$. $\blacksquare$

(Check with the standard formula: $S_n = \dfrac n2\bigl[2a + (n-1)d\bigr] = \dfrac n2\,[6 + 4n - 4] = \dfrac n2(4n + 2) = 2n^2 + n$.)
